name: The Cottage
tagline: Built by hand, with friends, in the hills
story:
I met Sem and Dafne while volunteering in Hampi. Back story matters — I learned through them that you can travel, build, and live fully in tune with nature and your own emotions. We were constructing a small stone pond that summer: cooking together, swimming in the Bhadra, exploring the rocks and temples around us. No alcohol, no substances — just the quiet of working with your hands, growing your own food, learning Italian cooking from Dafne, and stone philosophy from Sem.

When they visited me later in Chikmaglur, we decided to build something together. After a humble new year, we started on a wooden cottage. Stones as foundation in two-foot-deep holes, then wood frames — ten by ten, though it came out maybe ten by eleven.

In ten days we had a floor and four pillars for a roof. When they left, I had to find the momentum alone. Working solo can be daunting. The rains came and vehicles couldn't reach the site — everything had to be carried up by hand. Two heavy generators lugged up because there was no power for tools. Somehow, before the monsoon fully arrived, I got the roof on with help from my dad and his people.

Walls went up. Old windows were salvaged and fitted. The cottage found its shape. It's still not finished — but it stands.
closing: A quiet place to think, built with people I'll never forget, in a landscape that shaped how I understand shelter and belonging.

name: Coffee
tagline: Roasting in the town where it grows
story:
I grew up in Chikmaglur — one of the oldest and finest coffee-growing regions in India. The smell of coffee cherries fermenting on a neighbor's estate, the mist sitting on the Baba Budan hills, the red and green of the harvest season: these are things I've known my whole life.

But I only started roasting my own beans a few years ago. Home roasting is a different relationship with coffee — you see the full arc of transformation. Green beans that smell grassy and almost floral, then the building heat, the first crack like popcorn, the oils rising, the color shifting through cinnamon to city to full city dark. You make decisions constantly: when to pull, how long to rest before you grind.

I started with a modified popcorn maker, then built a small drum roaster from a salvaged motor and a perforated cylinder. Most batches teach me something. A few batches are exceptional. All of them are mine.

Chikmaglur coffee is grown by people who've tended these estates for generations. Being able to take that raw ingredient and bring it through one more step — that feels like the right way to live in this place.
closing: Roasting taught me that patience and heat are a form of attention. Every cup is a decision made earlier, fully committed to.

name: Mud House
tagline: Building shelter from the earth beneath your feet
story:
Mud building is one of humanity's oldest crafts, and one of its most misunderstood. In Chikmaglur, the old houses are built from local red laterite soil, rice husk ash, and jaggery water — materials that breathe with the weather, stay cool in summer, and require no cement, no steel, no supply chains.

I got interested in mud building after visiting a friend's cob house near Mysore. I started small: a garden wall. Then a tool shed. Then something more ambitious — a small room with thick walls and a lime-plastered interior, built almost entirely from the soil I dug from the foundation trench.

The work is slow and physical. You learn to read soil: the clay content, the shrinkage rate, the way to do a jar test to understand what you're working with. You mix with your feet. You layer and compress. You wait for each section to cure before building higher. There's no shortcut that doesn't weaken the wall.

Mud building made me a better programmer, somehow. Both require understanding the material deeply before trying to shape it. Both reward patience over cleverness.
closing: A mud wall that stands is a quiet argument: that the old ways have engineering inside them, and that beauty and permanence can come from the ground under your feet.

name: Ceramics
tagline: Hands, clay, fire — and a lot of patience
story:
I came to ceramics sideways, through a friend who had a wheel in her studio in Bangalore. I expected it to be meditative. It was, eventually — but first it was humbling.

The wheel is unforgiving of inattention. Clay centers when you're calm, and collapses when you're not. It took weeks before I could open a consistent cylinder. Months before I could pull the walls thin enough to feel elegant. I still lose pieces to cracking, warping, uneven bases. But each failure teaches something specific and clear, which I find satisfying in a way that other kinds of failure often aren't.

I work mostly in terracotta and stoneware — coffee mugs, small bowls, a series of vessels loosely inspired by the shapes of the Bhadra river stones I grew up collecting. I fire in a small kiln shared with other potters in a collective space in Chikmaglur.

Ceramics is slow in the way farming is slow: you invest effort into something that won't reveal itself for weeks. You wait for the bisque, then the glaze fire, then the cooling. And when you finally open the kiln, you find out what actually happened.
closing: Clay taught me that making beautiful things requires accepting that you cannot fully control them. The imperfection is part of the work.

name: The Farm
tagline: Growing things, sensing things, caring for the land
story:
I've been planting trees since I was a teenager. Mango, jackfruit, silver oak, and dozens of native forest species that take thirty years to matter. There's something about planting a tree that calibrates your sense of time — you're doing work that your future self, or someone else's future self, will benefit from.

The farm in Chikmaglur has expanded over the years: coffee plants, pepper vines, vegetables, a small nursery where I propagate things from cuttings and seed. My dog runs the fence line every morning and believes she is personally responsible for the health of the property.

A few years ago I started adding small electronics to the land. Soil moisture sensors wired to ESP32 boards that send readings to a simple dashboard — so I know which beds need water without walking every row. Temperature and humidity loggers in the coffee shade. A rain gauge that logs to a spreadsheet. Nothing sophisticated, but useful in the way that paying attention is useful.

The technology doesn't replace being in the field. You still have to go look. You still have to smell the soil and feel the leaves. But the sensors catch things you'd miss: a slow dry spell building in a corner, a section running wet after heavy rain. Data and instinct, together.
closing: The farm taught me patience on a scale that software can't. A tree planted today is a twenty-year conversation. I'm still learning how to have it.
